title: Ambrose
wiki_lead:
Ambrose of Milan (Latin: Aurelius Ambrosius; c. 339 – 4 April 397), canonized as Saint Ambrose, was a Roman theologian, statesman, preacher, and Bishop of Milan from 374 until his death. Trained in rhetoric and law, he served as Roman civil governor of Aemilia-Liguria at Milan before being unexpectedly chosen as bishop by popular acclamation in 374. His preaching, ecclesiastical activity, and writings made him one of the most influential Christian figures of the 4th century. 
As bishop, Ambrose became a prominent defender of Christian orthodoxy, particularly against Arianism, while also attempting to mediate the conflict between the emperors Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus. He opposed the execution of Priscillianist heretics and later excommunicated Theodosius following a massacre, maintaining that "an emperor is within the church, not over it." He was also a strong advocate of monasticism and asceticism, and his theological activity helped interpret and transmit Eastern Christian theology to the Latin West.
Ambrose left a substantial body of writings. Among his important works were De Virginibus (377), on the literal and metaphorical significance of virginity and purity; De Sacramentis, which contains the earliest witness to the present Roman Canon of the Mass; and the ethical treatise De officiis ministrorum (377–391), concerned especially with the conduct of the clergy. His exegetical writings include the Exameron (386–390). Ambrose was also the author of at least four hymns, including "Veni redemptor gentium", which form the core of the corpus known as the Ambrosian hymns, alongside other hymns traditionally attributed to him. He exercised a notable influence on Augustine of Hippo, whom he helped convert to Christianity.
In Western Christianity, Ambrose came to be recognized alongside Augustine, Jerome, and Pope Gregory the Great as one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers. He was also one of the four original Western Doctors of the Church, formally declared Doctors in 1298. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodox Church, Anglican Communion, and various Lutheran denominations, and is the patron saint of Milan and beekeepers. His feast day is usually observed on 7 December.

Background and career

Legends about Ambrose had spread through the empire long before his biography was written, making it difficult for modern historians to understand his true character and fairly place his behaviour within the context of antiquity. Most agree he was the personification of his era. This would make Ambrose a genuinely spiritual man who spoke up and defended his faith against opponents, an aristocrat who retained many of the attitudes and practices of a Roman governor, and also an ascetic who served the poor.


Early life

Ambrose was born into a Roman Christian family, of Greek descent, in the year 339. Ambrose himself wrote that he was 53 years old in his letter number 49, which has been dated to 392. He began life in Augusta Treverorum (modern Trier) the capital of the Roman province of Gallia Belgica in what was then northeastern Gaul and is now in the Rhineland-Palatinate in Germany. Scholars disagree on who exactly his father was. His father is sometimes identified with Aurelius Ambrosius, a praetorian prefect of Gaul; but some scholars identify his father as an official named Uranius who received an imperial constitution dated 3 February 339 (addressed in a brief extract from one of the three emperors ruling in 339, Constantine II, Constantius II, or Constans, in the Codex Theodosianus, book XI.5). What does seem certain is that Ambrose was born in Trier and his father was either the praetorian prefect or part of his administration.
A legend about Ambrose as an infant recounts that a swarm of bees settled on his face while he lay in his cradle, leaving behind a drop of honey. His father is said to have considered this a sign of his future eloquence and honeyed tongue. Bees and beehives often appear
grok_lead: Aurelius Ambrosius (c. 339/340 â 4 April 397), commonly known as Saint Ambrose, was a Roman Christian bishop, theologian, and statesman who served as Bishop of Milan (the city's patron saint) from 374 to 397. Born in Trier to the Roman prefect of Gaul, he trained in law and rose to become governor of the provinces of Aemilia and Liguria, where his reputation for fairness positioned him to intervene in the contentious episcopal election following the death of the Arian bishop Auxentius in 374. Though unbaptized and not ordained, Ambrose was acclaimed bishop by acclamation from both Nicene and Arian factions seeking a neutral arbiter, prompting his swift conversion, baptism, and consecration within days. As bishop, Ambrose staunchly opposed Arianism, the heresy subordinating the Son to the Father, through doctrinal treatises, persuasive preaching, and political advocacy that convinced Emperor Gratian to prohibit Arian worship in Milan and influenced Theodosius I to perform public penance after the Thessalonica massacre. His pastoral strategies, including the composition of Trinitarian hymns and the introduction of antiphonal singing drawn from Eastern practices, fortified Nicene orthodoxy among the laity during sieges of basilicas by Arian sympathizers under Empress Justina. Ambrose's exegetical sermons on Scripture, emphasizing allegorical interpretation harmonious with reason, played a decisive role in the conversion of Augustine of Hippo, whom he baptized in 387 after resolving Augustine's intellectual objections to Christian doctrine. Recognized as one of the four original Latin Doctors of the Church alongside Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory the Great, Ambrose's works, such as De officiis ministrorum on clerical ethics and De fide defending Trinitarianism, profoundly shaped Western moral theology, liturgy, and ecclesial governance.
